claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 has a high-temperature BCC state.
Phase stability in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is governed by diffusion-limited Al segregation.
Limited Al diffusivity during cooling produces local Al enrichment.
Local Al enrichment reduces the nucleation barrier for secondary-phase formation.
Local supersaturation together with slow Al redistribution controls the onset and fraction of secondary phases.
Rapid quenching from approximately 1300 °C preserves the high-temperature structure.
Lower-temperature annealing produces local Al concentration fluctuations and nanoscale clusters through limited Al diffusion.
Atomic mobility, particularly that of Al, is reduced at lower annealing temperatures.
Reduced atomic mobility at lower temperatures leads to local Al segregation.
A critical local Al concentration exists at which thermodynamic driving force overcomes the nucleation barrier.
Crossing the critical local Al concentration produces nanoscale FCC or intermetallic secondary phases.
Rapid quenching prevents Al segregation and preserves a single BCC phase.
Decreasing annealing temperature will increase the secondary-phase fraction relative to a sample quenched from 1300 °C.
Increasing annealing hold time from 0.5 to 2 hours will increase the secondary-phase fraction.
A sample rapidly quenched from 1300 °C will show minimal Al segregation and minimal secondary-phase nucleation.
The proposed effect may be negligible near the melting point or at very short annealing times.
At extremely low temperatures, grain-boundary diffusion or other kinetic factors may become dominant.
XRD and TEM can identify and estimate secondary-phase fractions, while atom-probe tomography can map local Al concentration.
The absence of systematic Al enrichment and secondary-phase growth across the stated time-temperature treatments would falsify diffusion-limited Al segregation as the governing mechanism.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis says limited Al diffusivity during cooling causes local enrichment, whereas the mechanism and baseline say rapid quenching, which imposes the strongest kinetic limitation on redistribution, prevents Al segregation. The role of diffusion limitation versus available diffusion time is therefore stated inconsistently.

The mechanism attributes segregation to reduced mobility at lower temperature, while the prediction asserts that decreasing temperature increases secondary-phase formation. Without an explicit countervailing temperature dependence of thermodynamic driving force, reduced mobility would ordinarily impede the redistribution required for segregation, so the proposed temperature trend is mechanistically inconsistent.
